blocks.x: Now what is your full name? My name is John Frank Casim. John Frank Casim. And where were you going? I was born in Yardall.
I was born December 17, 1898.
And what street were you born on? 737 Pine Street.
From the floor.

Oh yeah, I know where that is. I'm black on the side of the floor. Were you a family musical at all? Uh huh. Your family musical. Oh my brother never played with you. Oh yeah. Oh my people played with my dad. He played with old Pickford family. What instrument?
Melancholy.
That's called Melancholy. And who? Did he play any in the dance orchestras? String bands?
No, it was brass bands. Just brass bands? Yes, he taught us to play brass bands.

When did he die? Or is he still alive? My daddy died around 1931. And how old was he when he died? He was 54 years old. Uh huh. 54. Was he an ear man or a reader or both? No, he was playing a band. He was a player. But he didn't fake it all? No, he was reading them 6-8-Modges. Oh yeah, that's it.
Old man Humphrey used to teach the bandies.

Which Humphrey is that? It went out for him grab call. I had to take letters from the grab call. Oh yeah, you mentioned that. Is that Jim Humphrey? The old man Jim Humphrey. Oh yeah. If you want to stop at any time we can't have a phone lines or anything. We can't. Okay. Okay. You see that a lot of people playing music? Uh huh.

Yeah, my brother was playing. Bill Kazma, one of the best talent players they had. He used to go to Walter Pichon on the boat. And uh, quite a lot of you out there, they go playing every night. I'm not playing. Bill Kazma, they played a ton of slacks.
That's up in Chicago, man. Chicago, yeah.
And uh, Sam, he out in Chicago. He played guitar. He played Walter Pichon out in Boca.
He recorded for Bill Russell, you know what I'm saying? With Natty Dominique's band? Huh? He recorded with Natty Dominique's band in Chicago with Bill Russell. Sam, he hit all that.
Yeah.
I guess they all made a lot of records, huh?
Yeah, Mr. Russell don't go for it. Good kids open and Williams, the best talent player they had. I heard a lot of people talk about him.
That's right. Any other friends play? No, there's no one. I got any more friends. Sisters? Us three actually. No. My cousin, Chuck, he plays bass.
Oh, what am I telling you is he's a cousin? My first cousin, my cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin.
My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin. My first cousin.
My first cousin. We brothers and children.
I didn't know that.
We were first cousins.
I had no idea. Well, let's see now. How long did you take lessons from Jim Humphrey? About five years. About five years. You must start at your own, I guess. Four years, I taught.
My daughter, I was young, I was 19. About 19, 1918.
Around 1918? During the war, I was in the war, sir.

Yeah. I taught her how to play in Tickets or Lessons. I taught her playing the brass band over the river, old man, Leonard Allen. And the client that I got, he got that pawn shop, he got that pawn shop, probably seven and a half. Then I bought him out, a piece of equipment there.
What kind of clarinet was it?
At an E flat I got there.
You started on Lessons on the E flat or the B flat?
I started on the B flat but I bought it on the E flat at Coyne's or a ramp or a tree, the whole town. You got started with Henry Allen.
I started playing.

I tried to find a walk, I couldn't make a note, but I couldn't walk. Watch another fellow. And the Santa Father can't get out there playing a little funeral. You got to learn how to play a funeral. You got to learn how to play a funeral. Any God to know that, you got to learn how to play a funeral.
How long did you stay with Owen Allen? About four or five years.

Then I started playing with Henry Red Allen, his son, you know. Me and him and Johnny had a little four piece band. He was in short band, really. A little four piece band? A little four piece house band. I had Mitchell in the band, got Lucha on, Albojack on, Tramble. We got a little six piece band. We got all them jobs going down to Delco Island. Who's Mitchell?
We just get plenty of jobs. Who's Mitchell? Did you say you got Mitchell in the band?
Simon Phil Mitchell, bass player, he died too. Oh yeah. And Albojack on, Triumph on, Johnny Thomas on the drum. And Leonard Boccaf playing with Vagio. We just get plenty of jobs.
Did you know this bass player named Basie? Yeah. Basie Mitchell? Basie. I wonder if he was related to that Mitchell you just mentioned, Simon Phil.

I had a fella called I.T. Mitchell kind of him. He had his fingers all from snow like this. He got a good bit. He died, he died on drum energy. And he was cutting them samples of them Mitchell. That dog fella. He died. Probably the same time.

And how long did you play in the dance band? Remember what year that was? Oh we kept a dance band by five or six years. And then Henry Allen behind him, he kept behind him. He got better than us, you see.
And then we got on the boat and just put a high and put the sun on the boat, and the sun on the boat, and the rain out. And then he got better than going.
Who was he on the boat with? Huh? Who was he on the boat with? Who was he on the boat with? Who's man on the boat? I was going to go to Faith Morgan.
Oh yeah. Faith Morgan. He had some of the rain out on the boat, Faith Morgan. I had to make one or two trips on the boat, that's all.
He was gone. He was gone. Gone. And then who did you get on the trumpet?
Oh then I started using a tall fellow called Mud Quarter. He called him Kenner. He had a Wichita, Kansas now. Tall, skinny, skinny.
Back to your days before you played, who did you listen to before you started playing the instrument?

Who I listened to. So I'd take the lessons for some of them. Then I'd second on watching Johnny Dobson, you know. Played Kid Oda or whatever, doing the parade. Jack Kerr and I'd second watch it. Just watch the glider piece. I like glider piece, just watch it.
I wonder if you played E flat or B flat?
I played B flat in the orchestra, E flat on the parade. No, I mean Johnny Dobs. He played at B flat class.
In the street and everything, huh? Yeah, B flat.
Johnny Dobson, B flat. We never had no E flat. Who else did you see in the street?
What other? I wanted a band. Joe Watson played the class. The old tuxedo band.

He had E flat with a tuxedo band and a B flat in the orchestra. So I could follow him sometime. None of them don't apply like Johnny Dobson. That tonation was there. Yeah. Do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do.
That tonation. Oh, that tonation. Yeah. Yeah. Fair enough.

I did all that. That tonation. It's like I play a funeral parade. The tonation out there is that time. That's the principle thing about playing. And what about Johnny Dobson? Did he have any special numbers? Johnny Dobson?
Did he feature, was featured on the street?
Yes, he had featured on the street. any of them. Yeah. Yeah. See, they took Johnny Dotson.
And what about Johnny Dodson? Did he have any special numbers? Was he featured on the three?
He hadn't featured any of them.
Any of them? It didn't matter, huh?

Yeah. See, they took Johnny Dodson. They had sent him to Bishop playing with the kid over the band. Bishop would blow him up, so when he'd blow him up, I mean you'd get drunk and come on to jump. He'd say, man, it took Dodson to make a clown at play. But it took Dodson to make a clown at play. And that's Bache to run. If he wants Bache to play tonight, you gotta bring him in. Come on, man. Get something to play. Come on, man. Like something like that. Keep him out of heaven. He'd go on somebody's guard and they'd go. He'd go on a rope up in his back pocket and all that. He got tired of it.
Did Bache play any good? Yeah. Did Bache play any good?

Yeah. Bad son of a couple. You had to keep him. Keep him right to get him half drunk to keep him. Come on, man. Get another shot. You'd bring him on the job, wouldn't you? Had to be gone with somebody. Blur anybody up. Played so much cladier to put him on some pralice slacks, you know. Didn't that an issue?
Who were some of the other good clarinet players for Ragtime?

Ragtime? Yeah. Yeah. George Barkey. I didn't know him. I was too young to be. I'm 60 years old. I was 17, 17. Young guys way, way older than me. Reds and Teow in the front. They put their music all the time. Peekoo in the front. They had their music up in the front. That's young players that me got it. What about Blind Freddy? Did you ever hear him? Blind Freddy. Blind Freddy. Blind Freddy's got all the time. That's tall. Did you ever hear him play? That's the only place I've got it.
What about Blind Freddy? Did you ever hear him?
Blind Freddy? Blind Freddy's got all this giant stuff. He's got 12 days here. Did you ever hear him play?
Never heard of him playing except harmonica. But harmonica? Young harmonica?

That's the way he plays. Time to meet two days after he hit, 45. He'd stand on the corner. He'd get right there on the corner. He'd play the horn like he played harmonica. He plays too. It's a gift he got. He's playing the Liberty Bell Band.
Who was that? Westlitt Downer? Westlitt Downer, that's right.
Down at Kilpin, Baton Rouge. That's the trumpet player.
Eddie Marsh went to the trombone play.
Eddie Marsh, he played Kid Poinsett.
Oh yeah.

But Eddie, what the dialer player out there in Baton Rouge was a took jaw from him. Eddie Marsh played around him with Kid Punch in there. He's a good company man. Getting old now. Kid Punch. He's somewhere in the out of town.
Oh yeah, I got his address if you have a loan.
On Ramport Field. Yeah, you got it?
I got it.
I got it in the Rocks in the hotel then? Somewhere around.
Yeah, in the Rocks in the Rocks.
Yeah, I'm a punch in the union man. I don't know. No, he's not straight with the union.
No.
Plenty of guys out in the union, they're doing that business. They're working. Yeah, they got to stay straight with that union.
Yeah. Now let's see. Who did you play with after you left Allen's brass then? After they left Allen's brass, I started playing the record brass.
Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. We put this march up to call Longfellow, 432. Longfellow's march was a real player of the pure. We went to the Shire, you know, everything started playing. La, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da. Joy looks, you know what to make there. But no doodle-doodle-doo there, you see. You play what you see there already. The fella said, well, what's the more I see tomorrow? I said, maybe about what? Oh, maybe that man can't really say, I don't think about it. But no man can do. I said, you know what see me now? I'm a very young child. I don't know. Everything, everything.
Since that time. About what time was that?

By the way, about your schooling, how did you get your schooling? Did you go to a Catholic school or a private school? I went to Magdine 24th, private school. I went to 7 school. Did you go to the Catholic schools at all? I went to Catholic school. I called him Cameroon and called his son John LeVoy.
I made my first communion.

Did they have any music in school? They didn't have any music in school. You had to pick it up on your own. I just wanted to check on that one point. Let's see, we've gotten into brass band. We've gotten you out to organizing your own young tuxedo. You've had that ever since you organized it. Was that before the depression? That you organized the young tuxedo? Young tuxedo? Yeah. After the depression. It was after the depression. You were playing in the WPA band at the time?

I was playing in the WPA band. I wasn't playing in my band. I was playing in WPA band three years. But on the WPA I was working. One client, one client player, one more. I was right there to see Mr. Morton.

I was staying there three years. I see. And how long had your young tuxedo been going when you joined up with the WPA? Oh, mine and my band were by the WPA. It came after the WPA. It came after the WPA. It came after the WPA. I see. I think so. Well, who was Mr. Martinez?

I was a hitman over the WPA band. Direct. Supertender. And who was underneath him? He had a court lady, Pinchback 2, who was directing the band. He was marching with the Superbody. And after they put him down and put him on the bench, he took a lady called Mr. Ralph. The big Ralph talker. She was directing. It's another director. What would y'all play? We'd play all of them six days of the Moises, of course. We'd play songs after. We'd go in the morning for two hours. We'd go in the old Lord and the poor, right? We'd play that concert that evening for two hours. From seven to nine. I mean, from ten to twelve nights then. And they'd go home and get out there from three to five. We'd go rehearse that morning from nine to twelve, three hours. Would you have a play of dance? We'd rent the tune act up. We'd go rehearse that. We'd run over to the beach, get them straight. We'd go to Chad Hawke. We'd go to the boys' home. We'd go to the boys' home. Yeah. We'd go to the boys' home. Yeah. But never play to dance. Mm-hm. Never play to dance with them. Mm-hm. Never play to dance with them. She was rehearsing, and we run over to the piece, get them straight. Better go to Chad Hall, go to the two to four, like that different jailhouse on a Monday night, seven or nine. Went to the boys' home. Yeah.
But never played a dance, people didn't? Never played a dance with them.

Oh yeah, the men would play dancing. They'd play a different office. I'd be another man here, Mr. Miller or something. They'd turn all that money in. Lewis walked out every dance he played in the book, every dance he played. We'd turn the money, we'd just show it. Yeah.
Well, after you got out of the WPA, did you play in the street any then? Oh yeah, I was playing.
I was playing in the street, a different band I loved. Sort of spotting, huh? Yeah, things were slow.
Mm-hmm. The job was being or something. Mm-hmm. And then, how long before you got a steady job on the street?
I had no steady job. I played on the radio. I mean, you weren't regular with any band?
Yeah, I was playing Wood and Joy,

I played on the two-day, five or seven, so Jake Grappin' and two-day and Fibon. I played there about two years. Mm-hmm. We were in the United States. Yeah, but I mean, you weren't with any street band steady, any brass band steady then? Oh yeah, I was playing with the band.
And the old Tuxedo band, the Rikker, the Rikker friends, the old Tuxedo band. Oh yeah.
The Rikker friends, the old Tuxedo band. Oh yeah. That's David. The old Tuxedo band, the Rikker friends, the old Tuxedo band, the old Tuxedo band, the American mother. Oh yeah.

That's David. He's the old Tuxedo band. Mm-hmm. Who was in Wood and Joy's band that you were playing with? Me and Wood and Joy's band that you were playing with? Well, me and Wood and Joy's band were in the boxing shop and the bill go.
Wood and Joe and Brad went to O'Connor with the human man and gave us there. Played for the Zulu, you know. Just two corners.
But you just had four pieces with Wood and Joe then. Yeah.
Me and Clyde with John Cornet, and walked the person on, on Vanjo, where my brother Joe Kevin ran from. He died for a spot. Mm-hmm. He was a good guy.

Mm-hmm. What did Wood and Joe play like? Mm-hmm. What did Wood and Joe play like? What kind of style did he have? He was telling me Wood and Joe play like? He was telling me Wood and Joe play like? What kind of style did he have? He was telling me Wood and Joe

would be a good colliner player. I don't know. Mm-hmm. He could play a corner to him. He would pick it up and all the stuff. Well, he played a straight corner. Strong. Straight, strong, strong. Powerful man, of course.
He played a lot of play. He played a lot of play. Much variations?
No.
No, mostly lead.
I don't know the corner. I tell you he's a good colliner player. Yeah. I got mostly, Wood and Joe's a good colliner. Mm-hmm.
He played mostly lead then on the corner. Yeah, mostly lead on his corner.
Strong.
Did he use much mutes? Mutes, nah, and then.
He could throw. You got Joe from the other player.
Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.
Five left, wouldn't you? You know he'd ask me to ask him. Yeah.
Well, who did you have in the young tuxedo when you first organized it?

First I could play with him. Mm-hmm. I had a, a platonic called Page on the studio for him. And Albert Jackson on the trombone. Mm-hmm. I had Joe Avery on the trombone. Mm-hmm. And my cousin was alto sax timbres. Mm-hmm. I had a little Jim on the bass drum. I was using a Latinx's piece. Oh, my kid, I used no smear, you know. Oh, my kid, he's very terrific. I like to have a young tuxedo thing. That's right. Right. Right. And then they had the two lads. Yeah. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Right. Landry, Rodgers, and Big Eady Jones and I play in my band. I was talking about playing. They had the jaunts working in the woods. Come ask me, by my hand, look man, can we come with y'all? Landry, Rodgers, and Eddie Jones. I took them in my band.
Didn't have a baritone or an offer?

I used to use Peter White sometimes on baritone. Boy, they bought flowers on the nose. They bought flowers. See, the ripper bag used to buy a buddy out of four. I knew Jamaica called Flowers. We run on the ship. I didn't see any good ones. But a telephone and a baritone, that's a brass band. But now I got that outdoor site in the tennis center. They got they something about it. You can't get the other player now to Peckhorn. I said, oh, the harmony, oh, the music is in Peckhorn.

Well, that about brings us up to date on the brass bands, I think. Huh? We know pretty much what's happened since then. So I got a reference to that, I've written down. Now, did you play with many other dance bands other than your own? Oh, yeah, I think. You know Chris Kelly? I heard of him. Chris Kelly, like, got some money. He said, guys, they're triple the money. Can't keep nobody.
How's the bond? You play a trombone. Mm-hm. money can't keep nobody. How's the bondage of their tram? You know the fat out of it, good tram. We talk good tram.
And who else was in the band? Have a piano player or not?
They used piano players, Sam? Piano player? Mm-hmm. I'd use piano players sometime.
No, I mean Chris Kelly, did he use it?
He would sometime? Yeah, George E. Popper used to play with him.
Oh yeah.
He thought about that and all that.
That happened to me. I saw George E. Popper the other day.
George E. Popper died, didn't he?
No. I saw him at Eddie Pearson's Wake.
Yeah? He's crippled, man. He crippled? He saw a brosket.
Yeah, I got his cord in my pocket. I thought he died. No, man. Huh. Did he have a good drum, Chris, regular?
Chris Kelly? Yeah. Yeah. Dave Bailey on the drum. That fella played bass drum, a jumper, a Nickerson band.
Gibson band. Yeah, Gibson.

Where does Dave live now? I don't know where Dave's live. Somehow it's fun. But Dave really good trap drum, too. Dave is old, I'm telling you. Dave Bailey got a good age. Well, I'll have to dig up his address.
I'll ask Eddie Richardson Hill, I guess. Dave Bailey. You might have it out of you, bro. Yeah.
You're looking at it. Because I know he's an old-timer. Dave was an old-timer.
Mealy Barnes tells about him. Yeah, Mealy Barnes is good. Clive with Chris, too. He's an old-timer.

Chris Kelly, Dave Bailey on the drum. Yeah, I know he's an old-timer. Mealy Barnes tells about him. Yeah, Mealy Barnes is good. Clive with Chris too. He's an old-timer. He's an old-timer. He's an old-timer. Mm-hmm. Was Mealy a good clarinet playing? Yeah, we were a ragtime player. Mealy Barnes is an old-timer.
Who was your favorite clarinet player for blues? Speaking of ragtime players, who could play the blues more? I don't know.
I was a blue rider. I saw a Georgia boy. He was a great kid. He was a great kid. He was a great kid. Well, back to Chris Kelly.
Did he have a banjo player? A bass player? Banjo. Yeah, banjo player. Which a boy called Alex Statt used to play bass with.

And banjo, you know, he seemed to Chris could do the other band. Mm-hmm . Did he have a good funeral? Hmm? What kind of funeral did he have? What kind of funeral, man? He paid the Arnold back. Chris Keller, Sam Morgan, and Lorde Duran. He paid with the Arnold, Chris. Oh, man.

Joe Watkins, he was very glad he was. Did you work at Chris's funeral when he died? Hmm? Did you work at Chris's funeral when he died? I'm not afraid at Chris's funeral. Did you work at René's funeral?

Right? And then I'll be there when I'm with Chris Keller. I don't know. I didn't play that cue. He died downtown. I played Chris Keller band, all the oil up and all the trombones. Poor's his brother, oil up and all the trombones. Poor's his brother, oil up and all the trombones. He was away from me. The weather played Clyde, see? Poor's a great trouble. Poor's a great trombone. Yeah. I ran up with him. He was a great team. Mm-hmm.

Now, who would Chris play for? What kind of people? Hmm? What kind of places would Chris play in? Who would he play for? Who would he play for? Oh, he'd go to Santa Sons and Copper Riven Hall and E. Codd Hall. He'd go to high and more around. He'd go to high and more. Was Chris a flashy dresser or did he dress for playing?

Yeah, he was a tractor. Chris Kelly. Chris Kelly. Sam Moore and Chris Kelly had a crowd of all the kids right there. And they went in and they put a package on. Well, they're using one cornet long days or two. Huh?
How many cornets would they use? One or two? One. One.

Some type of piano is every piece of that. Yeah, he was a tractor. He was a tractor. Chris Kelly. Chris Kelly. All the people would go to that. Sam Moore and Chris Kelly had a crowd of all the kids right there. Anyway, they put a package on. Well, they're using one cornet long days or two. Huh? How many cornets would they use? One or two?
One. One. Cornet, trample, clanded, banjo, guitar and bass. Sometimes he pianists every piece of that. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . What are some of the other dance bands you played? What are some of the other dance bands you played?

Well, I was playing with Mud Quarter and then a band grew up in the North. So the wick stopped, I'd go with the man and get the wick, you know. If you want to get no job, come and dig all over and throw it back to the wick. I'd get a job I'd hide and throw it into it.
And after you left Mud Quarter, did you go with it?
Scrapped around and made up two jobs I wanted to see. Oh yeah. That's it.
That's the best girl. Henry Payne. What was Cato's name? Did you know his full-on name? Who name?
Cato.

Louis Cato. The snare drum player. Louis Cato. Louis Cato. Yeah. Louis Cato. Louis Cato. The snare drum player. Louis Cato. Louis Cato. Yeah. If we can locate him. What are some of the different clubs you played for at Connell time? One played for the Eleanor.

Mm-hmm. The Eleanor club. They played for the large clubs. They played for the buttons. They played for the Zulus. They played for the Zulus. They played for Zulus. They played for Zulus. Mm-hmm. They played for Zulus. They played for Zulus. They played for Zulus.

There was one thing I wanted to ask you about. Two. What goes on at Connell. What kind of music do you play on Connell Day? You don't play Derriges, huh? You don't play Funeral Marches. All Ragtime. All Ragtime. All Ragtime.
What's on? I want you to play blues and songs and all that. Mm-hmm. I want you to kill out my marching. I want you to want to jump.
Mm-hmm. Now what about a cornerstone line? What would you play?
Well, play songs till you get there. When you get there, I want to take those playing hammers. They're all hammers. Yeah. Yeah.
You start out on a cornerstone line where? At what point would you start out? Would you start out at the clubhouse or?

I'm going to leave from the club to go to the church and the other store, the ground and the other store. Yeah. I'm going to leave there with a hammer, you see. Play more soil and hammer till I get there. Then I'm going to go ahead and get ready to lay the stone and play a funeral marches. And then after the stone was laid, do you stay at the church or do you go back to the club or what? Well, you'd be finished at the stone leading. I see. Then we'd be marching back in. Every red ring would be marching back to the field. Most of the time, just after bringing that stone and being finished.

Now, how do you get your sheet music for the young tuxedo? How do you get your music for the young tuxedo? You told me you order that and then sometimes... I stand up and get my hand. Yeah, but some of it you told me it was written out by a guy. Who would write it down? Oh, sure. Louis Dumaine. Louis Dumaine, huh? Louis Dumaine, huh? You paid $4.39? Yeah. That's one.
That's one arrangement? Two. Two of them. The eternal last rest, the eternal peace. Mm-hmm.
Where did Dumaine get the idea to arrange this? Louis Dumaine, he'd copy some songs, stuff like that, the band's out, you know?
He died. He spread the old tuxedo. Mm-hmm. He...
Where would he get these songs that he'd copy down to?
Well, he'd buy a little piano copy at the military store, like, you know? Oh, I see. He'd write everybody a little part of it with heifer mouches or that. Oh, I see.
Would that be hymns and songs called?
He'd buy hymns after hymn books, too, and write a thing. Yeah, and he'd buy songs, too.
Mm-hmm. I never heard any of his songs, but I only heard the hymns.

Well, yeah, he died, you know, a little too many times. He'd play the Eddie Jack, the old tuxedo band, and I'd have to... Yeah, and he was leading the band. Pa George was playing solo, Lewis was leading. And he was using shots, Lewis Madison was the old tuxedo. Lewis DeBan was leading the old tuxedo band. Oh, yeah, in the late days. And Celestane wasn't playing at all, then? No, Celestane. I played with the brass band. Eddie Jackson was running the band, that was... Oh, I got the idea, man. Yeah, I knew it to make the lead to the band.

Now, say on an average funeral, how would you... How does that happen? What happens first on a funeral? Where does the band go to start? When the band goes to start, you can see the band will meet at the hall. They meet at the hall.
Yeah, at the hall. Well, I already mentioned all the square foot. You know, it would be ready to be for him once.
Mm-hmm. And the club and the band. The club and the band.

The club and the band are going ready to be, everyone. Mm-hmm. They go to the church, the undertaker to get the body. Go to the undertaker to get the body, and then... Go to the church, you get the care to dismiss it. Mm-hmm. Make the round with that second line, come on in.
Now, when you go from the hall to the undertaker, what do you play? Say, the first piece, what would be a gift?

Well, sometimes they're watching them coming out with the body. Then, at least you need to feel like pulling out, you know? Mm-hmm. Please avoid and tell you please last rest. Mm-hmm. Put them a good over there, they're putting them good over there. Put them a good over there. It be a funeral march or a hymn. You know, it got to be a funeral march coming out with the body. Yeah. The whole time a funeral march. They play a hymn going to the kingdom. Mm-hmm. It almost takes you to the death of the wild, to the Lord, Lord. Believe me. Say anything you want, then you go out and get them. But you got to feel a funeral march coming out with the body. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. And then you take the body to the church. And what do you play on your way to the church?
Take the body away?
From the undertaking to the church. To the church. Well, they play a funeral march all the way.

They get on the side and get ready to take him out and bring him with you. Then another funeral march to bring him with the church. Get ready to play a funeral march and bring him out to the church. You only got that body, you got to play a funeral march. Mm-hmm. After you dismiss that body, they play a hymn. When he's gone, they start to play a rag thing. Oh, yeah.
